title: Light in the Darkness
summary: The passage describes earlier affliction in the lands of Zebulun and Naphtali and the way of the Red Sea beyond Jordan in Galilee; it then speaks of people in darkness seeing a great light.

explicit_facts.text: The land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali were lightly afflicted at first, and later the affliction was more grievous by the way of the Red Sea beyond Jordan in Galilee of the nations.
People who walked in darkness have seen a great light; light has shined on those dwelling in the land of the shadow of death.

reasonable_visual_inferences: A symbolic contrast between darkness and light can convey the passage's imagery.
unspecified_visual_details: The identity and appearance of the one who afflicts the lands.
The people’s identities and appearance.
The physical appearance and source of the light.

narration.text: The people that walked in darkness have seen a great light

doctrinal_or_story_notes: The light is described as shining upon people; no visible divine appearance is specified.
prohibited_inventions: Do not depict the reported afflictions as a newly occurring present-time event.
Do not assign identities to the people or the afflicter.

title: Joy and Release
summary: The passage describes a multiplied nation and increased joy, then speaks of a broken yoke, shoulder-staff, and oppressor’s rod.

explicit_facts.text: The nation is multiplied and its joy increased; people rejoice before God as at harvest and when dividing spoil.
The yoke of burden, staff of the shoulder, and rod of the oppressor are broken.

reasonable_visual_inferences: Harvest rejoicing and the breaking of a yoke may be represented symbolically.
unspecified_visual_details: The nation’s identity, clothing, and surroundings.
Who breaks the yoke and when.

narration.text: Thou hast multiplied the nation, and increased the joy
For thou hast broken the yoke of his burden

doctrinal_or_story_notes: The broken burden is presented as poetic imagery.
prohibited_inventions: Do not stage a specific battle or identify an oppressor.

title: A Child Is Given
summary: The text contrasts the noise and bloodied garments of battle with burning and fuel of fire, then proclaims a child born and a son given, with government upon his shoulder and titles named.

explicit_facts.text: The warrior’s battle is described with confused noise and garments rolled in blood; this is contrasted with burning and fuel of fire.
A child is born and a son is given; the government shall be upon his shoulder, and names are given: Wonderful, Counselor, The Mighty God, The Everlasting Father, The Prince of Peace.

reasonable_visual_inferences: The contrast between battle and burning may be conveyed with non-graphic symbolic imagery.
unspecified_visual_details: The child’s identity, appearance, location, and circumstances of birth.
The person or object bearing the stated government.

narration.text: For unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given

doctrinal_or_story_notes: The birth and titles are proclaimed in the passage; it does not narrate a birth scene or describe an appearance.
prohibited_inventions: Do not depict the child or assign the titles to a visible person.

title: A Kingdom of Peace
summary: The passage describes the increase of government and peace without end, and a kingdom established with judgment and justice forever.

explicit_facts.text: Government and peace increase without end upon David’s throne and kingdom, established with judgment and justice forever; the Lord of Hosts will perform this.

reasonable_visual_inferences: A throne or kingdom may be represented as symbolic imagery, without depicting a specific ruler.
unspecified_visual_details: The appearance of the throne, kingdom, or its ruler.

narration.text: Of the increase of government and peace there is no end

doctrinal_or_story_notes: The verse is prophetic description, not a narrated enthronement.
prohibited_inventions: Do not depict a coronation or identify a visible ruler.

title: The Word Comes to Israel
summary: The Lord’s word is said to have been sent to Jacob and to have lighted upon Israel; the people, including Ephraim and Samaria, are described as speaking in pride.

explicit_facts.text: The Lord sent his word to Jacob, and it lighted upon Israel.
All the people, including Ephraim and the inhabitants of Samaria, shall know; they are described as speaking in pride and stoutness of heart.

reasonable_visual_inferences: Light may be used symbolically for the word lighting upon Israel.
unspecified_visual_details: Whether Jacob or Israel refers to a visible individual or group in this passage.
The appearance and setting of the people.

narration.text: The Lord sent his word unto Jacob

doctrinal_or_story_notes: The word lighting upon Israel is figurative language.
prohibited_inventions: Do not depict the Lord or Jacob as visibly present.

title: The People’s Boast
summary: The people boast that fallen bricks will be rebuilt with hewn stones and cut sycamores replaced with cedars.

explicit_facts.text: The people say fallen bricks will be rebuilt with hewn stones, and cut sycamores changed into cedars.

reasonable_visual_inferences: The boast may be lettered over symbolic images of bricks, stones, sycamores, and cedars.
unspecified_visual_details: The speakers’ identities and appearance.
The location and whether rebuilding is actually underway.

spoken_dialogue.text: The bricks are fallen down, but we will build with hewn stones;
spoken_dialogue.speaker: The people

doctrinal_or_story_notes: This is a reported boast, not an account of construction happening.
prohibited_inventions: Do not depict the rebuilding as a present event.

title: Adversaries Gather
summary: The Lord is said to set Rezin’s adversaries against him and join enemies together; Syrians from before and Philistines from behind devour Israel, while the anger and outstretched hand remain.

explicit_facts.text: The Lord shall set Rezin’s adversaries against him and join his enemies together.
Syrians from before and Philistines from behind shall devour Israel with open mouth; the anger is not turned away and the hand remains stretched out.

reasonable_visual_inferences: The named groups may be represented as opposing forces in a symbolic composition.
unspecified_visual_details: The appearance of the forces and the location of any confrontation.
The appearance of the hand.

narration.text: The Syrians before and the Philistines behind

doctrinal_or_story_notes: “Devour Israel with open mouth” and the outstretched hand are figurative expressions.
prohibited_inventions: Do not depict literal devouring or an unmentioned battle.

title: The People Do Not Turn
summary: The people do not turn to the one who smites them or seek the Lord of Hosts; the Lord is said to cut off Israel’s head and tail, branch and rush in one day.

explicit_facts.text: The people do not turn to the one who smites them or seek the Lord of Hosts.
The Lord will cut off from Israel head and tail, branch and rush in one day.

reasonable_visual_inferences: Head and tail, branch and rush may be shown as symbolic imagery.
unspecified_visual_details: The identity of the one who smites the people.
The specific events represented by cutting off.

narration.text: For the people turneth not unto him that smiteth them

doctrinal_or_story_notes: The cutting off of head and tail is explained in the following verse as referring to people.
prohibited_inventions: Do not depict an unmentioned execution or physical cutting.

title: Head and Tail Explained
summary: The ancient is identified as the head and the prophet who teaches lies as the tail; leaders cause the people to err, and those led are destroyed.

explicit_facts.text: The ancient is the head; the prophet who teaches lies is the tail.
The people’s leaders cause them to err, and those led by them are destroyed.

reasonable_visual_inferences: Leaders and followers may be represented as a symbolic group without individual identities.
unspecified_visual_details: The identities and appearance of the ancient, prophet, leaders, and followers.
How destruction occurs.

narration.text: The ancient, he is the head
For the leaders of this people cause them to err

doctrinal_or_story_notes: Head and tail are explicitly explained as figures for people.
prohibited_inventions: Do not depict literal body-part transformations or specify a manner of destruction.

title: No Joy or Mercy
summary: The passage says the Lord will have no joy in the young men and no mercy on the fatherless and widows, describing everyone as hypocritical and evildoing and every mouth as speaking folly.

explicit_facts.text: The Lord shall have no joy in the young men or mercy on the fatherless and widows; everyone is described as a hypocrite and evildoer, and every mouth speaks folly.
The anger is not turned away, and the hand remains stretched out.

reasonable_visual_inferences: Young men, fatherless children, and widows may be shown only as representative groups if depicted.
unspecified_visual_details: The people’s appearance, setting, and any specific speech.

narration.text: neither shall have mercy on their fatherless and widows

doctrinal_or_story_notes: The outstretched hand is figurative language.
prohibited_inventions: Do not invent dialogue for the people or depict a divine figure.

title: Wickedness Burns
summary: Wickedness is compared to fire consuming briers, thorns, and forest thickets; smoke rises, the land is darkened, and the people are compared to fuel for fire.

explicit_facts.text: Wickedness burns as fire, devours briers and thorns, kindles in forest thickets, and they rise like smoke.
Through the wrath of the Lord of Hosts the land is darkened, and the people shall be as fuel of fire; no man shall spare his brother.

reasonable_visual_inferences: Fire, smoke, and darkness may be used as symbolic imagery for the passage’s figures.
unspecified_visual_details: The land’s appearance and whether any literal fire is occurring.
The people’s identities and appearance.
doctrinal_or_story_notes: The passage uses fire as a figure for wickedness and its consequences.
prohibited_inventions: Do not present the metaphor as a literal supernatural event or depict graphic harm.

title: Hunger and Division
summary: The passage describes people snatching and eating without satisfaction, then names Manasseh and Ephraim as against one another and together against Judah; the anger and stretched-out hand remain.

explicit_facts.text: A person snatches on the right and remains hungry, eats on the left and is not satisfied, and people eat the flesh of their own arm.
Manasseh and Ephraim are against each other and together against Judah; the anger is not turned away and the hand remains stretched out.

reasonable_visual_inferences: The hunger and tribal conflict may be conveyed symbolically without depicting bodily harm.
unspecified_visual_details: The identities and appearance of any people shown.
The physical setting and any specific conflict.

narration.text: and they shall not be satisfied
they together shall be against Judah.

doctrinal_or_story_notes: Eating one’s own arm is figurative language; the passage does not narrate literal self-injury.
prohibited_inventions: Do not depict literal cannibalism, injury, or an unmentioned battle.
